utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before the Cermak will call its next witness, there's a tiny little procedural matter which the Chamber would like to raise not because we think there will be a lot of comments on it. Usually, exhibits in a case which has not yet been concluded, although being public documents, usually no copies are provided to third parties. They can look at it, there's nothing -- but copies are not provided. Exceptions are made now and then, if there's a specific request. There was a request by the media or at least a newspaper - I'm not even informed about what it exactly is - to receive a copy of the Kovacevic expert report, D1676. The Chamber has consulted on the matter. We do not see any reason why this document, which has been extensively dealt with in court, why it should not be given to a party who is apparently interested in receiving a hard copy. Any comments from the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We have no objection either, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the Chamber advises the Registry that the Chamber would agree with providing a copy of D1676 to interested parties, more specifically, media. Are you ready, Mr. Kay, to call your next witness or would it be you, Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. It's just the issue of the transcripts from yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Do you want to settle that now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In essence, I have agreed with the Prosecution on the pages, and this was your request that in essence the particular page that the Prosecution referred to be given some context, and I have agreed those pages with Mr. Hedaraly. For P2640, in the English transcript, it would be pages 69 to 71, and that's the page numbers both on the documents and in e-court; they're identical. And in the B/C/S that would be pages 69 to 71 and the corresponding pages, the ERN numbers for that, because there are no page numbers on that document, the corresponding ERN numbers, the last four digits are 7544 to 7546. So that's for P2640. For P2641, and there I would just point out to the Court that the particular context of the comments that Mr. Skegro said at the time concerned the refugee problems in Croatia. This is where he was talking about people not being able to live together, that those comments were provided to you in isolation, and actually if you look at the transcript, what's being discussed by the president and his ministers are the problems with refugees leaving Bosnia and going to the coast in Croatia and there being public disorder problems. And so the pages that I have put in actually address that and the Chamber can read it. But it's English pages 27 to 30 on the document, and in e-court that's pages 28 to 31. And then in the B/C/S, it's pages 35, line 5 to 39, line 18, and the corresponding ERN numbers are last four digits 6493 to 6497. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And they will be -- or are already uploaded together with the cover page, because we're talking about the minutes of meetings held with the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'll make sure, if they've not been already uploaded, that they are uploaded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because there we see who's present and we have a date --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and we have what the document is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I do not remember whether we had already assigned numbers to them. But they have to be uploaded anyhow in the limited version. Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It's just easier, we could just replace the existing numbers for the full document with the extracts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It was a rather silly remark I made because we talked about P2640 and 2641, so numbers have been assigned to them. But now they will be uploaded in their limited version, cover page, and the pages the parties have agreed upon, which give sufficient context for the Chamber to understand the testimony and also contains those portions on which the witness specifically commented. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I have a different issue to raise so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This matter being raised, could the parties inform the Registrar and the Chamber once the new versions have been uploaded. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, just on behalf of the Gotovina Defence, over the last few days we have seen Exhibit P463, which is the transcript with Mr. Radic, and there's been some discussion about the 10 per cent figure and it has been assumed that that was a reference to not allowing more than 10 per cent to return. And I just wanted to note that we understand that's the Prosecution's interpretation of the document; we have a different interpretation of what that document is. We would like to at least put our position to the Chamber when -- either now or whenever the Chamber feels it's convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Wouldn't it be best that we are referring to this document now and then, that the parties try to find, I would say, as neutral as possible description of that document which then preferably is to be used when the document is put to a witness. And there's always a possibility that if we want the witness to look at the text itself, then, of course, that can be put to him, but that we don't have quarrels about the way in which you refer to the document is wrong because we understand the document to be a different one, and, of course, just referring to a document by number, which, of course, is also a way, but it is not very informative for the one to whom this document is presented. Is there any way of resolving it in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we, of course, will be happy to speak to our colleagues with the Prosecution about the issue. I do wish to point out that -- just that, very briefly, our interpretation is that the discussion there is about moving more Croats in so that -- if you have a thousand Serbs there and you move 9.000 Croats in, they become 10 per cent of the population and not preventing return. But I will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you cannot agree, then the Chamber would appreciate to receive from both parties a brief description of what this portion is about, and then the Chamber will see whether it can find a -- as neutral possible characterisation of summary, or -- well, a text which refers to that portion of the document. So if the parties could not agree, the Chamber would like to receive their, not more than ten lines, description of what that portion of the conversation is about. Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. President. Although I suspect we will not agree on the interpretation, I'm sure we can try to at least find a way that we can characterise the document if it will be referred to in a general way rather than the specific language. But we will talk to our colleagues from the Gotovina Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I'm not expecting the parties to agree on the interpretation at this moment, but to agree on a formulation which gives sufficient information in referring to this document and that portion of the document. If there's no other matter, then, Mr. Kay, the next witness the Cermak Defence calls will be ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's Mr. -- it's Mr. Rincic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Rincic. Before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration of which the text will now be handed out to you by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rincic. Please be seated. Mr. Rincic, you will first be examined by Mr. Kay. Mr. Kay is counsel for Mr. Cermak. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Rincic.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If the Court could produce on the screen a document, 2D00719.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Rincic, you're looking at some papers there. Can you close them, please. I know that's a hard copy of your statement. Don't worry about that. I don't think you have been in this courtroom before, but in front of you are two screens, and on the right-hand side, you will see a screen containing a document in your own language soon. If you just look at that. Mr. Rincic, do you recognise a statement there that you gave to the Cermak Defence which has been signed by you?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in relation to that statement, is it correct that there are certain corrections you would like to make?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we go to paragraph 20 of the statement. And can you see the text there in your own language, and can you see paragraph 20?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Within that sentence, there is a -- within that paragraph, there is a sentence containing the figures 2 to 3 per cent. It's on line 9. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And in the statement signed by you, it says: "General Cermak and all of us who attended these meetings believed that 2 to 3 per cent happened of everything that actually had happened." Did you want to make an explanation to clarify that sentence further?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: During the first couple of days, we heard and we noticed that there was shooting and there was smoke at a distance, and we could hear shots coming from a distance. And we believed that certain things were happening, certain incidents, related to war. We believed that this was the sequelae of the previous war activities. It was only later, a few days later, that we realised that things were not what they seemed initially, that things were different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there another amendment to your statement that you would like to make, in relation to paragraph 22. If that can be put on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In the English, please. In the Croatian, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to that paragraph, would you like that paragraph taken out and deleted because it is inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be noted for the record. Were there any other corrections or clarifications that you need to make, in relation to your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes. In relation to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: In relation to the report on the repairs done to the electricity grid in certain villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What would you like to say about that? Is that a matter that's in your statement, relating to the repairs to the electricity? You're going to be looking at a document in a moment in relation to electricity. If could I ask you this question: Taking into account the corrections that you have made to this statement, is everything that you've said in that statement, as it remains, true and correct, to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: As far as my statement is concerned, everything is true and correct and to the best of my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to this statement, if we look at the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Croatian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We see that it is signed by you. And can you identify that as being your signature?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, all the pages in between are signed as well, and we've just seen one on the way. I don't propose to adduce each of them, with the Court's leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Without any objections from the parties, leave is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Rincic, if I was to ask you today the same questions that you were asked in the making of your statement, would your answers be the same today as when you gave them for the statement?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, they would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, in those circumstances, I move that this document be put into evidence as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Waespi. One question. Mr. Kay, you raised the issue whether there were any other corrections or clarifications. The witness said in relation to the report on the repairs done to the electricity grid in certain villages, and then we moved on without knowing exactly what the witness wanted to do. Mr. Rincic, would you like to change anything in your statement in relation to the electricity in the villages, or would you just give something in addition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not have in mind any changes with regards to what was said. I am convinced that everything that was said is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we don't have to pay further attention to it at this moment and it's up to the parties to see whether what you would apparently then like to add or further explain, whether they will ask you about that, yes or no. Mr. Registrar, the exhibit number for this document would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1680.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1680 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think all will become clear. As it's a document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, at this moment --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the witness expressed that he had further --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- comments or inaccuracies and before we decide to admit something into evidence, the attestations should be as good as they with be. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour, and thank you. In relation to this statement, there are two documents which are referred to which are not already court exhibits. There are other documents in paragraph 18 and paragraph 24 that are exhibits, but there is two other documents that are referred to in the statement. At paragraph 24, line 10, a pass referred to, 65 ter 529. Your Honour, I ask that that document be made an exhibit, as it's within the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1681.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And Your Honour, the next document, which is also referred to in the body of the statement at paragraph 17, in the first line of paragraph 17, you will see the number SVA2-107. That is a document, 2D00720. And I ask that that be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1682.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1682 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Your Honour, that deals with those matters in the statement. And then could we call up this document which I will ask Mr. Rincic to comment upon. It's 2D00286. And Your Honour will find at paragraph 15 in the statement, the area to which this refers to, which may deal with the matter raised earlier by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Rincic, can you see before you a document --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we just turn to the second page of it. Can you go right to the bottom, please, so that the signature can be identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you -- do you see your name there on the document?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we go back to the first page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you recognise the document?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this document is about.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: This is a report about the electricity grid in Knin and villages around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And we don't see a date on the document. But can you tell us, to the best of your knowledge and belief, when this report was written by you?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: That was sometime around the 12th of August, or perhaps the 13th of August. Or maybe even the 14th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Of course, I can raise it in re-direct, but if you go to page 2 in English, it relates to the dates of 24th to 27th of August, due to whether that's prospective or the witness talks about incidents that happened at those times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Great -- I'm grateful to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would you like to look at the second page of the report, Mr. Rincic? We can see a date referred to as the 24th of August to 27th of August. Can you just read that to yourself. Does that help you at all, in relation to when this report was written?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: It does. It does help, yes. And all that happened a long time ago, and obviously I've forgotten some things, and it is clear that this was written sometime around the 27th or the 28th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the purpose of writing this report, in relation to the power in the region was for what?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: The purpose was to inform my superiors about the situation in Knin, how things stood, and how the situation with the electricity power would develop.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, might this document be made an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1683.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1683 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There's just another document that I'd like to you look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we have on the screen, please, Exhibit D01036. And the Court may want to turn to paragraph 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if you look at the document on the screen in front of you, Mr. Rincic, can you see the Croatian document there? Can you look at it, please. If we turn to page 2 of the document --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can the Croatian document be engineered so that we can see the signature at the bottom rather than the text, please. Ah, page 3 in the Croatian, I'm advised. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you see your name there, Mr. Rincic?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you write this document?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you recollect when this document was written, as there isn't a date on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps if we can see the front page again.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I believe that this was drafted sometime between the 10th and the 12th of August, or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the purpose of writing this report, can you tell us what that was?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: The purpose, again, was to inform my superiors about the situation with regards the revival of economy in the municipality of Knin. I also wanted to inform Mr. Ivan Cermak about the same thing, because that was his prerogative. He needed to be informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this already an exhibit, so I -- I will ask no further questions about it. Your Honour, that concludes my direct examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Please wait there, Mr. Rincic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have no questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No questions. Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No questions. Mr. Rincic, since the other Defence counsel have no questions for you, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Waespi. Mr. Waespi is counsel for the Prosecution. You may proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Rincic.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'd like to cover a few areas with you in clarification of your witness statement and some of the things you said in examination-in-chief. But let me first go to the so-called deletion of paragraph 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So if we could get the witness statement on to the screen, that's D1680, page 6 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You recall, you testified that you wanted paragraph 22 to be deleted. Now, the witness statement, which I'm sure we'll get on the screen shortly, was only taken a few months ago, end of March, beginning of April, so what happened in the meantime? Or, in other words, why do you want this paragraph to be deleted from -- from the statement? Did you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Take your time. You can read it, of course, and I'm sure you remember it. It's the issue about the repair of the railway, and you go in quite some detail about how you went to see Mr. Ademi, the Chief of Staff of the Split Military District, or the duty officer at that time, and eventually got them to provide military security for the railway repair, and you go on in some detail about where it was, that it was surrounded by a forest, and so on, and so on. So why did you want this paragraph to be deleted today?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: The main reason why I believe this should be left out is that my private visits to the Military District to see Mr. Ademi and other officers got conflated with the other memories I have of these events. These were my private acquaintances; I knew them privately.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But -- please continue.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: So I conflated this with the official duties that I performed. The security provided for the repairs carried out in certain areas had to be sought by phone through duty -- through the duty service of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rincic. But do I understand you correctly, the events, as you described them in paragraph 22 - this may be 12 or 15 lines - they happened as you told them. This is correct? The only issue is that you don't want to conflate your private involvement, because you knew Mr. Ademi from before, with your official duties and you feel that's inappropriate. But the facts, as you have stated them, as you told the Defence, they are true and correct. Do I understand you right?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: No. What I said was true, but the statement I made that was written down here is a bit confused. I confused certain matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, please, what's confusing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I could, just as technical matter, I believe that the Prosecution hasn't released its documents in e-court yet. And if the documents could be released, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: It will be done instantly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean the documents for cross-examination? Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Rincic, please tell me, which bits are confusing? You can also start, and we have all time, to tell me which lines, which sentences of paragraph 22 is not confusing. Or you can tell us which are confusing, whatever you prefer.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: For the purposes of securing works that took place outside of Knin, I sought, through the duty service of the military police, whom I called over the telephone, that I be given a certain number of soldiers who would secure workers, making repairs out in the field of certain facilities or installations. This detail which is not contained in Article 22 is something that I remembered subsequently. When, six months ago, I spoke about the matters contained in item 22, I did not recall this important detail. I remembered only later on. And I've just told you what it is. It is a -- an important issue, and that's why I believe that item 22 needed to be left out. It had to do with the provision of security for works that took place outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thanks, Mr. Rincic. But help me, please, so I understand. In order to get these security troops to -- to guard the repair on the railway --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think the witness said military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I thought the witness said he called the duty officer of the MP but I might have ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, 18, line 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Maybe it is something that needs clarification. I don't want do interrupt my learned friend but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Anyway, I can pick that up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you called the duty service of the military police. Now eventually I understand that the security was provided, and my question to you is: How did you manage that? Did you manage by calling the duty service of the military police, or by, as you explained in paragraph 22, going to see Mr. Ademi, or the duty officer of that unit and get them to release the security, or did you do both, one as a follow-up to the other one? Do you understand what my issue is?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I understand your question. That's where the essential difference lies, as I've told you a moment ago. I told you that this was something I remembered later on. It was through the duty military police that I was given security details; whereas, the rest were my private contacts and private visits in the Military District.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But they did happen, these, as you call them, private visits to the Military District. You did go to see Mr. Ademi. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And did you talk to him or to the duty officer about providing security, or did that not happen?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to object. That mischaracterises what the witness just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I don't think the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- one second, I will re-read. The question may be answered. It -- you may repeat the question, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You told us that eventually, you know, security came, and one of the reasons was because you talked to the duty service of the military police. You also told us that you, indeed, went to see Mr. Ademi, as stated in paragraph 22. So my question to you is: What did you talk about with Mr. Ademi, when you went to see him. And the sub-question is: Did you discuss the release of security for repairing the railway?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: The issue of securing workers conducting repairs on the railway track was not something I discussed, was not something I discussed with Mr. Ademi because it was one line of my duty, which was of no interest to him particularly. Your question was what we discussed. We discussed matters that were of interest to me and which had to do with the life and work of military units in the field, and I was privately curious about the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'll follow up on that in a moment. But let me go back to Mr. Ademi or the duty officer. So you did not discuss with Ademi and also not with the duty officer the issue of providing security to the repair of the railway?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I did not --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So that's --

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: -- because I had already solved that problem before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Very well. I understand you better now. So that's one of the sentences which is not correct in paragraph 22. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, why did you tell that to the Defence when you met with them end of March, beginning of April of this year?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Because the events happened a long time ago - I'm referring to the events in Knin - and what I had as a recollection at the time was that this is the way things happened. Subsequently, I cast my mind back to these events and I realised that things were different.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did somebody tell you that things were not as you had stated them to the Defence, or was it your own volition that changed your mind?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Of course, it was of my own volition.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me go back to what you did discuss with Mr. Ademi, and I quote you: "We discussed matters that were of interest to me and which had to do with the life and work of military units in the field, and I was privately curious about this situation." Can you tell us what you discussed in -- in as much detail as you recall?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: What I discussed with Mr. Ademi and other officers in Military District -- well, first of all, I had taken part in the homeland war together with them. I fought side by side with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when you say "them," it's Mr. Ademi and whom?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Commissioned and non-commissioned officers, who were members of the 4th Brigade, 7th Brigade, who were deployed in the area of -- of Knin and around Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And so specifically going back to your discussion with Mr. Ademi, can you tell me what you discussed with him, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I was interested in knowing what the developments were in Knin, what the situation was like in the northern part, beyond Knin. As you know, in addition to Sector South, there was Sector North and other areas, where war activities took place and which were liberated. These were very eventful days bristling with information where one was interested in knowing as many things as possible, and where I knew that I would be able to get informed, I sought to get informed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Rincic, you have taken five or six lines to answer the question without really -- you told us now what you're -- that you had certain reasons why you would be interested but you still have not told us what you discussed with Mr. Ademi. What did you discuss? What questions did you pet to him, what did he say?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the witness has referred to these being a long time ago, and the question was prefaced by Mr. Waespi, if you recall, and a general answer is given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I disagree with you on the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the witness doesn't remember what was discussed with Mr. Ademi, he can tell us. And just tell us that you don't remember. The witness gave the reasons why he was interested in knowing what and where, et cetera, and that it was -- that these were very eventful days, and which gave information one was interested in. He did not -- and that was the question asked to him, he did not tell us what the content of the conversation with Mr. Ademi was. If you remember, would you please tell us, Mr. Rincic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I won't say anything but I do refer Your Honour to page 22, line 11. I won't say anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Kay. Could you please focus, if you have any recollection, what the content of your discussion was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was mostly discussed had to do with the -- my acquaintances and friends who were members of certain units. I was interested in knowing whether anyone had been wounded, lightly or seriously, whether anyone had been killed. There were several of my acquaintances and friends who had been wounded and killed. This is what most of our conversations revolved around. I don't remember the rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you remember when the meeting or conversation between you and Mr. Ademi took place, and also the location?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I don't remember when exactly. And it took place in Knin. Again, I don't recall the specific venue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the railway works, were they on the railway between Knin and Gracac?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: There too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you remember how many security troops, people, were eventually released to do the job alongside the railway?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Three to four; I can't remember exactly. Three to four soldiers, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were these normal soldiers, or were these military police?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to show the witness a document which just was brought to my attention, and obviously I haven't included it to the documents to be released but perhaps that might assist the witness in -- in his memory about who these soldiers were. This would be 65 ter 657, an order by the commander of OG West, Mladen Fuzul.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, it seems that we have two issues, the first to have it added to the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I take no point on this. Things arise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No point. Yes. Yes. You can put the document to the witness and ask questions in relation to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Witness, please have a look at the screen, and you see an order by the commander of OG West, Colonel Fuzul, and it deals with the release of 30 soldiers from the 134th Home Guard Regiment for railway works, and it's following the orders given by the commander of the Split Military District. Now, is this order in any way linked, in your opinion, about the railway works with which you were concerned or perhaps others of which you have any knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of this order. This is the first time I'm seeing it. This particular security detail was required for five days only; whereas, I -- my request had to do with a longer period.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you don't recall having had 30 soldiers doing security for railway works with which you were concerned with? Your answer is no?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: [In English] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit P2644.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2644 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the second point I wanted to clear up from what you said in in-chief was that comment, and it relates to paragraph 20 of your witness statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we could go back to D1680.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Where you originally stated to the Defence, and I quote: "General Cermak and all of us who attended these meetings believed that 2 to 3 per cent happened of everything that actually had happened." And I believe you said, on page 8, lines 2 to 5, today, that things were different to what they initially seemed. Can you please clarify what was different and how did they seem initially?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As stated in the transcript, as was written down in the transcript, initially, we did not have the information reflecting the state of affairs as they were. Subsequently, we realised that several houses had been burned and that there were instances of actions -- of unlawful actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you initially believed that the reports you received or the information was exaggerated; but, later, you realised that it was not. Is that a fair assessment of what your testimony is?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Initially, we had not even been receiving reports, and then, as soon as we received reports, we went through them and realised that some had reflected the actual events and that others were exaggerated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Let's turn to this issue of exaggerations and look at another example, which, I believe, did you not clarify. In paragraph 23 of your witness statement, you address the work of the ECMM. And it's in English at the end of page 6, about the fourth or fifth line. You say, and I quote you: "The monitors wrote reports about the crimes in the field without having checked the facts but on the basis of information given to them by somebody." And then you also go into an example of shelling information. Now, what's your basis for saying that? How do you know that, in your assessment, ECMM reported without having checked the facts?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I know, because it was dangerous to check the situation on the ground. And they were afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Who specifically was afraid? Can you give me any name?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's go to a similar issue. This is in paragraph 20 of your witness statement. And you state as follows, and it's in the middle of paragraph 20, where you see -- actually, just below the 2 to 3 per cent reference. There you say: "After about 15 days, Mr. Cermak started receiving letters of protest from UN workers about arson and looting in the field, and during the meetings he would forward that information to the chief of civilian police and the military police commander." How do you know which letters Mr. Cermak received?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I know because the coordination meetings aimed at reviving the Knin economy that were chaired by Mr. Cermak were the meetings that I myself attended. And Mr. Cermak briefed us about the letters at those meetings. He told us about them, and he forwarded those letters to the military police and all the other relevant bodies that had to be informed. In that way, he made sure, and he did his bit for such events to be prevented.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Are you confident having seen every single letter the UN wrote to General Cermak?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: There is nothing you can be 100 per cent sure about. So I can't be sure that I saw every single letter, but I saw the most important ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm just interested in your unqualified statement: "After about 15 days, Mr. Cermak started receiving letters of protest from UN ..."

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't have to be 15 days. Maybe it was ten days. I was talking in principle. It was after a certain time. For the first ten days or so, the figure that we were operating with was 2 to 3 per cent. We didn't know what was going on. At least from my point of view, I didn't know what was happening. Mr. Cermak, however, did [as interpreted] know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to go to P363. It's a letter. And it appears on page 5, both English and B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Rincic, soon you will see on the right side of your screen the Croatian translation of the letter, the original one, which is in English on the left side, and it's dated 11th of August, 1995. And it's a letter from the UN commander to General Cermak, and it says as follows, and I quote: "During our meeting yesterday, both Mr. Paavo Pitcanen and I brought to your attention information gathered by UN sources concerning the widespread and systematic looting and destruction of property, crops and livestock." And I skip one sentence, continuing: "Recalling your statements during yesterday's meeting concerning your honest efforts to control the situation, I again protest these activities and ask to redouble your efforts to prevent the organised destruction and theft of property." Do you recall, Mr. Rincic, being shown this letter from Mr. Cermak during one of your meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I can't say with 100 per cent certainty, but I may have and immediately thereupon, Mr. Cermak took steps. He informed the military police, and he called for an urgent action on their part, to remedy the situation, to curb such activities. I can see that this letter was sent on the 11th of August, and given the circumstances, three or four days, sometimes seemed as ten to 12 days, and that's why I'm not very precise as regards the dates, due to the heavy circumstances that surrounded us at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So we have to be careful in assessing your witness statement here when it comes to dates. Thank you, Mr. Rincic. Let me actually stay while we're on the topic of the meetings you had with Mr. Cermak, and I believed you called them coordination meetings. In paragraph 19 of your witness statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If we could revert back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You talk about the participants at these meetings. And the witness statement is D1680. Now, you say in the middle of paragraph 19, page 6 in the English, at the top: "It is important to note that people who were subordinate to Cermak, for instance, Knin garrison employees, did not attend these meetings." But there were people there who were subordinate to Mr. Cermak; for instance, like Mr. Gojanovic, Marko Gojanovic, who was his deputy. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Not always.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I have to correct myself. It's -- the gentleman is called Marko Gojovic and not Gojanovic. But when he was present, he would be a subordinate of Mr. Cermak being present at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was his deputy, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you remember whether Mr. Jonjic was present, if you know who Mr. Jonjic was.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What was his function?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know what the relationship between Mr. Cermak and Mr. Jonjic was?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I believe that Mr. Cermak was Jonjic's superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rincic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, it might be a good moment to have the break. We will have a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have a break. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, there's just one issue with the -- with Exhibit P2644. I would ask that it receive MFI status because I think the translation needs to be checked on the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I -- perhaps what I should have -- let me just ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The issue, Mr. President, I can draw your attention --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you'd give me one moment, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There is -- you're referring to 2644 and there being a translation issue. Of course, there's still a pending translation issue also on another document we mentioned earlier, that is P2640, where -- where the parties agreed, I think, on what the translation issue was. But a formal request for -- I do understand that the Cermak was intending to or even has already requested a formal correction of the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think there may be a little bit of confusion in this subject --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- Your Honour, as to the exhibits Your Honour has just mentioned there and the -- I think that we may need to look at it and just identify carefully what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm just referring to it, because earlier we were talking about selections, and apparently there may have been a translation issue there as well. Mr. Misetic, 2644, the translation issue --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is in the preamble. The order is not for the security of the final construction works. It's in order to secure the completion of construction works, and the difference is whether the troops are there providing security or they're there working as physical labour working on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I noted that in the order, the first item, that there the security was not mentioned anymore and that seemed to be, well, not to say directly contradicts but at least there was some tension between the -- what came before, where, clearly, security is mentioned in the English text; whereas, in the instruction given -- the reason why they are there, that there is the -- it's the construction works themselves and not providing security to those. So, therefore, it struck already my eye and it certainly is worthwhile to have it verified. Mr. Waespi, may I take it that you would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's on its way to Mr. Monkhouse already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's good to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we rise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Misetic, have we done with it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yeah, I just wanted to know if it would get MFI status, just so it wouldn't fall off the radar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar, would you -- for P2644, would you please change the status pending the verification of the translation into MFI. Yes. Mr. Registrar is nodding yes, so that's now on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's just a matter on the transcript and the translation issue at page 28, line 8. Mr. Cermak, however, did know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, one second. Let me just get that on my screen. 28, you said line 8. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: "Mr. Cermak, however, did know." Those Croatian speakers on my team have said that the word "not" was missing, that is to be found -- will be found within the audio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me then first perhaps verify with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: "Did not know, however," is what I've just been told is the phrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Rincic, I take you back to one of your answers: "The figure that we were operating with was 2 to 3 per cent. We didn't know," I take it, I have to read, "what was going on. At least from my point of view, I didn't know what was happening." And then you said something about Mr. Cermak. Could you repeat what you said about Mr. Cermak, whether he knew or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the first couple of days, Mr. Cermak, just like me, I'm sure, didn't know what was happening. He was not aware of those activities and events outside of Knin and around Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I take it that you never learned anything which might show that he knew, or did you learn that he did not know? I mean, if I say that someone doesn't know something, it could be two -- either he told me that he doesn't know, which is -- may be surprising now and then because how could you tell not to know something you apparently do not know. What was it? Did you never hear anything from him or did you never receive any information which would allow to conclude that he would have knowledge, or did you have specific information which would point at a lack of knowledge? Could you tell us what you meant by Mr. Cermak that, as you said, that you were sure that he didn't know what was happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sure that Mr. Cermak didn't know, because, during the first couple of days, we maintained very intense contacts, we talked a lot, we discussed things. We discussed the needs of pursuing various kinds of actions and taking various kinds of steps to provide for a normal life in Knin. Namely, with your leave, I would like to remind you that during the first couple of days in Knin the conditions were extremely difficult. It took a lot of effort, and before anything was done, a lot needed to be discussed and agreed, in order to tidy up all the streets and areas in and around Knin. The first time ever Mr. Cermak received information, he was very angry and very agitated, and that's how I know when he learned about those developments for the first time, and that's how I know that it took some time for -- for the information to reach him. And then he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you tell us when that was, in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most probably it was the letter that was sent to him by General Forand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The matter has been clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm grateful for Your Honour clarifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break and we will resume at 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I would just like to put on the record that where D1682 was not objected, that there was a formal request to have it added to the 65 ter list but that's included in admission that leave was granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, Your Honour. I forgot about that and I had it on my list to raise. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No problem there. Mr. Waespi, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Rincic, I'd like to talk with you a little bit about your background and the various functions you had, civilian and military. And I think we can get through this fairly quickly. And it's based, of course, on what you told us, what Defence in 1680, your witness statement. First of all, your military position in 1991, according to witness statement, and this is all in paragraph 1, you were the assistant -- you were an assistant commander of the 159th Brigade in Zadar. You were an assistant commander for what? What was your speciality?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I was the assistant commander for logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And from when to when was that?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I was in the 159th Brigade from the establishment of the brigade, and I believe that it was in the month of December 1991 to the month of August or September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And then at one time you became the commander of the 307th Brigade -- logistics base in Zadar. And from when to when was that?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: When the logistics base was established, which was sometime in the month of September, or maybe the month of August, 1991, until -- I apologise, 1992. Until the month of April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who was your superior at the time, when you were commander of the 307th Logistics Base?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I was the commander of the logistics base, and it was subordinated to the Military District of Split, by establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the commander was General Gotovina?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me turn to your civilian position. In 1993/1995, according to your witness statement, between - it's paragraph 1 again - between the 22nd of July, 1993, to the 30th of April, 1996, you were assistant minister of economy for special purpose manufacturing industry. Now, who was your superior, or who were your superiors?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: My immediate superior was Mr. Cermak; he was the minister of economy. After that, it was Nadan Vidosevic and after that it was Mr. Matesa, for a very brief period of time before he became prime minister. He was followed by Mr. Stern, and then during Mr. Stern's office, I was assigned to another duty. I left the ministry, which means that during my office, I went through four different ministers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I believe Mr. Cermak was your superior in 1993 while Mr. -- parts of 1993, while Mr. Vidosevic was your superior in 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's talk about your military position in 1995, and the attack on Knin or your -- as it relates to you on to Benkovac, you advanced to Benkovac. Now, you state in your witness statement, paragraph 9, that you wanted to participate in Operation Oluja, and you were the advisor for logistics in the 112th Brigade in Zadar. Now, when did you join them, and why?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I joined them two or three days prior to the launch of Oluja.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: And your question was why, and the answer is: I wanted to participate in the liberation -- liberation and re-establishment of an integral Croatian state.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Who was your brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Colonel Fuzul.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Wasn't he, rather, the commander of the operations group, and Mr. Ivkovic was your brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I really can't remember. However, I remember that I spoke to both of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But you cannot distinguish who was whom, what function Mr. Fuzul had, as opposed to Mr. Ivkovic?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I can distinguish between them, but I don't recall at this time. I didn't consider it important. I was not a classical soldier. I was a mobilised assistant minister, and a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what was your exact task as an advisor?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: During Operation Storm and the other combat activities during which I was in the army, I was in charge of logistics and had under me the entire brigade of -- providing logistics support. It belonged to the OG Zadar. I had extensive experience in providing logistics support during war operations, specifically during Operation Maslenica. We provided logistical support to 18.000 soldiers, all of whom were either deployed on the front line, on the move, or resting. They all had to be provided for logistically. They had to have food, footwear, clothes, ammunition and everything else that comes under the logistics department. Along the axis from Zadar toward Benkovac, where a great many forces were deployed, I was providing support in action and expertise, in an attempt to have all the soldiers participating in the operation at the time as equipped logistically as possible and as safe and secure as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just so I understand, because in your witness statement, paragraph 9, it talks about an advisory role, and, now, a moment ago, you said you were in charge of logistics.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I wasn't charged with that. You misunderstand me. I was there to provide assistance to logistics officers and others who were dealing with logistics. A word put in where -- where it's needed can go along way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What were the assets, logistic assets of the 112th Brigade, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: There was a logistics base that I was the commander of. It was alive and well and providing logistics support. It was 307th Logistics Battalion of the OG Zadar; I was its commander. The commander who replaced me was Zeljko Dilber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It was a base. The witness said logistics base.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So now we not only have you in an advisory role but you're now the commander of the logistics battalion of OG Zadar?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I was a commander before becoming Assistant Minister. I was the commander of the logistics brigade, until the month of April 2003 and Operation Storm took place in 2008 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thanks. We covered the phase 2000 -- 1992 and 1993. I'm really interested in your exact role as a logistical advisor in 1995, during the advance of the 112th Brigade, which you joined voluntarily, to Benkovac. Were you in command or in charge of anything at the time, or merely an advisor?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I was only an advisor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And my question back, and perhaps you can -- maybe you answered already. But the logistical assets the 112th Brigade had, was it a platoon, was it a few men, was it a company, was it a battalion; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I don't recall exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you don't know, after so many years, what you were advising about at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I can't recall the precise issues, but it must have been problems that arose in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's turn to Knin. I understand that, and in paragraph 9 of your statement, that you went to Knin the day after liberation, the morning of the 6th of August, but, as an assistant minister of economy not as a member of the Croatian Army. Now, why did you remove your advisor hat of the 112th Brigade and go to -- to Knin, back as an assistant minister of economy?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Because we had liberated Benkovac and Knin. There was no reason why I should continue as an advisor. I accomplished the desired objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you said that in paragraph 10 of your statements: "When I entered Knin with my friends ..." Who were your friends you entered Knin with?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly who they were. Some of my friends who were good at handling weapons. They were supposed to provide protection for me, and cover for me during our trip to Knin. Or, rather, I was there to protect their backs and they were there to protect mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Were these friends part of any military unit or part of the Ministry of Economy or something else?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: No, those were friends from Zadar. They were members of certain military units, but I can't remember which ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But they were in uniform?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I was in uniform too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now let's turn to your evidence about the position of Mr. Cermak. In paragraph 12 of your witness statement, the second sentence, you state as follows: "I know what the duties of a garrison commander were because there was a garrison command in Zadar." So that's the basis for you talking about the duties of a garrison commander, because you were, at one time, in a garrison?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: The town of Zadar, where I was the commander of the 307th Logistics Support Brigade, is a garrison. For the two years while I was commander there, the commander of the garrison was Brigadier Frane Saric. I knew all of his duties and tasks which had to do with care for soldiers to billeted in appropriate quarters, funeral arrangements for officers, et cetera. In fact, there were no daily goals. It depended on the run of the garrison and life of military units. I observed the garrison commander at work for two years, and I could see what he was doing and what his duties were. Before that, Saric was commander of the 159th Brigade for almost a year, and I was his assistant for logistics. I personally knew Saric very well, and I -- I was in daily contact with him during his term as garrison commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So that's the basis of your knowledge about what the garrison commander does, what the duties are, you're observing the gentleman you mentioned, Mr. Saric, back in 1992/1993?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you don't know what the regulations actually say about the duties of a garrison commander? You are not familiar with those?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I wasn't interested in that at the time. There was a war on and regulations was something I was least interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, the Chamber is wondering, what the exact knowledge of this witness about the tasks of a garrison commander, in addition to what he describes in his statement, how that would assist the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yeah, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now in paragraph 21, Mr. Rincic, the first sentence says: "Mr. Cermak was not superior to the civilian and military police." And in relation to the military police, you continue later in paragraph 21: "I know that the military police was directly subordinate to General Lausic and Minister of Defence, Mr. Susak." Now, how do you know whether Mr. Lausic or Mr. Susak was in command of the military police? Did Mr. Lausic or Mr. Susak tell you personally?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I knew them personally, but they did not convey that to me in turn. I know that the military police was subordinate to Mr. Lausic and Mr. Susak because, at the time when I was commander of the logistics base in Zadar, I was on friendly terms with the commander of the military police in Zadar, Captain Grancaric, as well as with the commander of the military police in Zadar at the time when I was the commander of the brigade. I knew that the garrison commander in Zadar could issue no orders to the commander of the military police in Zadar, or to the commander of the civilian police in Zadar for that matter. The fact is that, following its liberation, Knin had the same legal standing as all the other free towns in Croatia's -- Zadar, Sibenik, Split, Zagreb, all of which had the military police force and the civilian police force. Therefore, the civilian police in Zadar could not issue any orders to the military police in Zadar. Colonel - I can't remember his name at this time - but it doesn't really matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So, again, your knowledge about the relationship between Mr. Cermak and the military police or the civilian police stems from what you know from your time back in 1992/1993. Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. Based on my knowledge, back from 1992 and 1993, and based on my first-hand experience from Knin, during my stay there with Mr. Cermak and others in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But as you said before, you have not talked to Mr. Lausic about that, about the situation, as it relates to Knin 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Well, we were worlds apart. He was in his world and I was in mine. We didn't have occasion to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you don't know what General Lausic told this Trial Chamber about whether he commanded the military police or not, or whether Mr. Cermak commanded the military police or not. You are not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In relation to the subordination between Mr. Cermak and the military and civilian police, you also state in paragraph 21, and I think that's the last sentence: "Mr. Cermak ... could only ask them to do something." But you don't know, do you, whether Mr. Cermak actually ordered or asked the military police or civilian police something to do?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I know that he asked them to do things and he didn't order them, because he was not able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you give me a specific instance of fact when you saw Mr. Cermak asking the military or civilian police something to do?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: At the meeting, at the coordination meeting for the reconstruction in Knin, on the day when Mr. Cermak received a letter from General Forand, I believe, the commander of the civilian police was present, and he asked him to make sure that these things did not happen again. I saw that with my own eyes that he kindly asked him to make sure that it stopped. He wasn't able to order him anything. He asked for follow-up but it was all in the form of a request.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Who was at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: It was a long time ago. I can't remember all of the participants at the meeting. I know that there was me, and, among others, the commander of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Roman.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who else was present?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. There were four, five, or six of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what were the exact words Mr. Cermak used when he asked the commander of civilian police for something; can you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Come on, guys, do something, stop the arson, stop all these ill deeds, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So he was talking to Mr. Roman or Romanic. And to whom else?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: And the representative of the military police who was there. I don't recall his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you recall -- can you tell me the exact words he used?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I know for a fact that he said, Please, do everything you -- to make sure that it stops, for our sake.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And stopping what?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: The burning of houses and similar things. Killing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Killing of what?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Probably certain civilians who they believed were soldiers. I don't know for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Whom are you referring to when you say "they believed were soldiers." Who are "they"?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I think that "they" were the ones who did these things. It was a matter for the police to find out who they were. If I was able to tell you that, then I wouldn't be telling that to you but to those who need to hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And before Mr. Cermak could ask, in your words, the civilian police to do something, who relayed the information about the burning of houses and similar things, killing? Who said that at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly who raised the issue. As soon as Cermak heard that, that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you don't remember who raised the issue but you do remember almost exact words, at least the word "ask," from Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was so astonished to hear of these things happen that it remained etched in my memory, the moment when I learnt of these things. I was surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think you said a moment ago that this meeting was probably about the letter General Cermak received from the UNPROFOR commander, which was around the 11th of August; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you entered Knin on the 6th of August?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And this meeting now takes place on the 11th of August and you are astonished that somebody raises the issue of burning houses to you.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes. And we had a meeting on the 7th, and 8th, and 9th. Nobody had ever mentioned anything of the sort beforehand, and on that day, when we heard of these matters, when the letter arrived, we had Cermak's reaction to that. I wasn't aware of these things before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, would your opinion about Mr. Cermak's ability to issue orders to the civilian or the military police change if I would show you orders from Mr. Cermak, General Cermak, to the civilian police or the military police?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: You can show me the book of orders where Cermak may have issued orders, but I know what the state of affairs in reality was and I know that he couldn't issue orders to anyone, be it the military or the civilian police. I'm telling you what the actual state of affairs was practically speaking. Paper, what's on paper, that's quite a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you accept that, while he couldn't legally issue orders, he might have issued orders but that's just on paper. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: No, that's not what I'm saying. What I'm saying is something else. Those who did issue orders and who should have been issuing orders on paper and who were responsible for issuing orders to the military police and the civilian police, that they are the ones who you should put these questions to and not this boy over here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: By saying "boy," you're referring to whom?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I meant the Generals.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You're here to answer questions, and I'm questioning you about statements you gave to the Defence about the authority of whom you call "boys." Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I do understand what you're saying, but you are putting to me matters that I know for a fact do not stand as you put them, and perhaps you misunderstand me, perhaps I misunderstand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me just go back to my original point. Do you deny that there might be written orders by General Cermak to either the civilian police or the military police? Do you accept --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, sorry. With all respect for my learned friend, the question, "Do you deny that there might be written orders," I don't think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The answer can be -- if we put it in a direct way. Do you exclude for the possibility that written orders were issued by Mr. Cermak to civilian and military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not excluding anything. I only know this: Even if he had issued an order of that kind it would not have produced any effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, you -- if we would -- no, no. Yes. Now you had answered my question but you apparently anticipated the next one. You say it would not have any effect. Why not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because, for example, if I had issued an order for them to do something, the result would have been the same. Cermak was not in a position to issue orders to the military police. He was not in charge of the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
