utterances.text: Yes. Now, if you, nevertheless, would issue an order, what makes you believe that it would, under all circumstances, without any effect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because, in practice, I did ask and requested assistance, and based on that, the commander of the military police would approve that or not, or -- and then if he was able to help me, he would issue an order for assistance to be provided to me. I realised in practice that that's how things ensued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're describing, apparently, what you consider to be the proper way of seeking assistance. And you say since that worked, an order could not have been effective, which is a kind of logic which -- why you would issue an order if you would know that it would be without effect, under all circumstances? What's the -- does it make any sense to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It does make sense, Your Honour. It was a state of war and one needed to do things fast and efficiently, rather than linger on and wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, what you're telling us, since it was a war situation, you would have to act efficiently by issuing orders which would necessarily be without any effect. Is that the logic of your answer, or have I misunderstood you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the logic. One who is not authorised to issue orders must not issue orders. He can, but without any effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that is dictated by the war situation, which was asking for efficiency in doing things. Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's turn to your actual position in Knin. And I believe you just mentioned that you yourself asked or requested the assistance of the military police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you give me an example of -- of such an instance?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: We were supposed to go to a -- the source of the water for Knin, which was three or four kilometres outside of Knin, it was not working properly, and people from the water supply had to go there and try and repair it for water to start flowing through the pipes and reach Knin, and the security needed to be provided for those men. And then I asked the military police to provide that detail for us on the following day, because there was such a need. And then the commander of the military police assigned a few individuals who were escorting the work -- workers who needed to go three or four kilometres out of Knin and be safe while performing their task. That was in order to prevent somebody shooting at them from the woods or from a location nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the military police you asked for his assistance?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Not the commander. I always addressed the duty operations officer. I don't know who the commander was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of the duty operations officer?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: No. It was somebody else every six or, maybe, eight hours. It was always somebody -- somebody new.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How often would you use the services of the military police?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: There was that one instance with the water supply; another involving telephone cables; then there was the railway situation. As far as I can remember, it was three or four times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And all these three or four times you were provided with assistance from the military police?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I think that the civilian police officers helped me once or twice. It was either/or. It really didn't matter who they were, as long as they carried arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was ever a request from your side, either to the military police or civilian police, denied?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Not directly. Sometimes I had to wait for the service to be able to provide me with men. Sometimes I couldn't do things immediately the following day. I had to wait for a day or two and things needed then to be postponed by a day or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But you eventually got what you wanted.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you said in your statement, paragraph 14, that you wanted to open a Ministry of Economy branch in Knin. And I think you then go on to say that you were "... officially sent to Knin as coordinator for the economy." Now you were given two officers and a secretary as support staff. Do you remember the names and the ranks of these two officers?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't say that I was assigned officers. I got people from the Ministry of Economy, officials, civilians, and a secretary. They were not military officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In -- yes, there might be a translation or English issue. In your witness statement, in the middle of paragraph 14, it talks about two officers. But these were employees of the Ministry of Economy. And -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And they were assigned to you throughout the period you were in Knin?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You remember the names?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Oto Jungwurth, a man; Sandra, whose family name I can't remember at the moment. She was a lady whose name you can check with the ministry. It shouldn't be difficult. And another gentleman whose name I can't remember, but if need be, I can supply you with their names subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you also say -- state that you had the official Ministry of Economy stamp and the stationery with the letterhead. Now that very much looks like a civilian position you had at that time in Knin.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But how come, then, that you signed documents on behalf of General Cermak, and you signed them -- and we have seen a couple introduced in examination-in-chief. You signed these reports on the official Knin garrison command letterhead as a Colonel Rincic. How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Because of the war situation that was still pretty much on, in reality, to provide for the effectiveness and the speed when it comes to dealing with problems. When something had to be done, using Mr. Cermak's name did the trick. Mr. Cermak's name was very strong, so using his name would get things done much faster than using the title the Ministry of Economy. I hope you understand me when I say that his name was strong. He was respected. And if I needed something to be done quickly, I would use Mr. Cermak's name. If I hadn't, things would not have happened as quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I think you said earlier, you yourself were in uniform at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: In the office I did not wear a uniform, and I did not carry arms. However, if I had to go on a field mission, I would wear a uniform for my own safety. I felt much safer wearing a uniform than wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I believe on occasion you did introduce yourself as Mr. Cermak's assistant or deputy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Not officially. In my official capacity I never introduced myself as Mr. Cermak's assistant. Perhaps -- no, I didn't. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But, unofficially, it's possible, as you recall today, that you might have introduced yourself as the assistant or deputy of Mr. Cermak?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I did not introduce myself as such. However, in some dangerous situations I wanted to make that impression, because it made me feel safer. When my life might have been at risk, I felt safer if I made such an impression. My life was at risk, you know. As a civilian, I could have been shot at.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Rincic. Two final topics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, if you have dealt with this topic. Could I seek clarification of your last answer. You said: "As a civilian I could have been shot at." Could you explain who would shoot at you as a civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it could have been anybody, on any of the sides, in confusion, in fear. Maybe they could have perceived me as -- as threat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The enemy troops remained behind in the woods or in some other areas, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you would expect them to first fire at civilians, but wearing a military uniform, you would not be a target for enemy troops? Is that how I have to understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's what I believed at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's go to the issue of the Tvik factory. In paragraph 25 of your witness statement, you talk about that, and I think one of the reports you introduced -- or which was introduced with you, talked about the factories. In paragraph 25, you say -- state as follows, the last five lines: "I was very pleasantly surprised when I went to the Tvik factory which was manufacturing ammunition for the RSK army and the JA and saw that more than 800 machines were intact and in working order." Now, when did you go to the factory?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Two or three days after my arrival in Knin, when I started working on reviving the economy in Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how do you know that the Tvik factory was manufacturing ammunition?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: In two ways. There were two things that confirmed my knowledge about the production of ammunition. First of all, we found some incomplete, unfinished ammunition of different calibre, and they were never finished because the production was interrupted by Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: And the second thing was that we found in the administration building a thank-you note from Captain Dragan, who is currently in Australia, as we know. He thanked Tvik factory for the assistance in supplying his units. And we also found a thank-you note from some other units; I can't remember which ones exactly. They also thanked Tvik factory for supplying them with ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you tell that to the gentlemen who interviewed you on behalf of Mr. Cermak, when you met them end of March, early April, that you found thank-you notes from Captain Dragan thanking them for supplying his units?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: No. They didn't ask me that so I didn't tell them. But the thank-you note is still there with Mr. Bozo Jusup in Zadar, who is the managing director of Tankerkomerc. He wanted to keep it as a souvenir. It still exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Bozo Jusup, he is living in Zadar?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Jusup, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can you get these notes, these thank-you letters?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: If he still has them, I might. You know, all that happened 15 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I thought you said a moment ago it still exists.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: It was just my assumption that it still exists, my assumption that he still has those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, these unfinished ammunitions, what kind of ammunition was that you saw when you visited the Knin factory -- the Tvik factory?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I saw casings for automatic weapons in baskets, in -- in a very large number. For machine-guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And why do you say these casings were produced in Tvik, in the Tvik factory? Did you see machines?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You have --

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Tvik is a huge factory. It has all sorts of machinery, presses, metal machines. I was the Assistant Minister for special-purpose production, for the production of ammunition, grenades, machine-guns, ammunition, and I know that Tvik could produce all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't get that. You were the Assistant Minister for special-purpose protection for grenades, machine-gun ammunition?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's the first time I hear that.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Wouldn't it be something worth mentioning in your witness statement, the official title of your role as an assistant commander? I just don't see in your --

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- witness statement any mentioning that you were the assistant minister for special purpose in relation to grenades, machine-gun, ammunition. But perhaps you can guide me. Perhaps it's a translation, or interpretation issue?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: It must be there. Let me -- let me show you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I may assist, Your Honour, paragraph 1, and line 12 and 13 of witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, half of it, apparently, is there. Special-purpose manufacturing industry. It says special purpose which is certainly an indication --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm looking at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- which goes in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: -- looking at the Croatian version of the statement of the original one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there a difference?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No, there is no difference, but there's a special wording in it which, for the native speaker, is almost at the first sight clear what kind of production is. So "namjenska proizvodnja" means exactly -- but I think that the witness could explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the issue only was apparently credibility of the witness. Mr. Waespi, do you want to further explore that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, no, I'm -- I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- or do you accept that at least --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- special production is specifically mentioned in the witness's statement as -- as part of his responsibility although not with the details, as he just told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me go back to the machine. So you're saying when you visited the Tvik factory, you say that you saw that casket full of machine-gun ammunition and you saw machinery capable of producing that?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you make a report about that?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't necessary. I didn't think that it was necessary, you know. It was a notorious fact that in the so-called Republic of Srpska Krajina that they were manufacturing for their so-called army, and at the moment when I found that, I did not see anything out of the ordinary. It was normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You went -- you were sent down there to check the state of the factory. And I suggest to you it was certainly very, very useful, even for the Croatian Army, having liberated this area to know that there is still an existing machinery capable of producing ammunition. And you're the specialised minister, as we just heard. You didn't think it was important to bring that to the attention of your superiors?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: No. I believed that that factory was extremely important for us and that's why Minister Vidosevic appointed me as the president of the steering committee of that factory, where over 300 people found employment in a very short period of time. I was the coordinator of the revitalisation of the factory. It didn't -- really did not matter to me what the factory was producing for the Republic of Serbian Krajina. What mattered was what the factory would go on producing for the Republic of Croatia by -- it was a matter of bygones and I wanted to face the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just to clarify your question [sic]. Your first words in your response, you accept that you did not inform your superiors that you found a functioning machine capable of producing ammunition in the Tvik factory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Those were universal machines that were capable of producing nails, bolts and casings. Those were not special machines that could only produce weapons. A good handyman could produce even a violin on any of these machines. I only reported back to my superiors that the machinery was good, in working order, and that we could use it for anything, and I left it to them to see what they wanted to do in the factory. And they decided -- I did report back to my superiors what kind of machinery I found on the ground and what they were capable of producing. What I said, that it didn't matter, was what had been produced in the past. To be honest, I could not even say with 100 per cent certainty that they had produced ammunition, because I wasn't there. I did not witness that with my own two eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You just saw a functioning machine there, capable of producing anything from a violin to a grenade?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps that's a good moment, Mr. President, for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have a break and we'll resume -- could you give us an indication, Mr. Waespi, as to how much time would you still need.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's only about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And looking at the other parties, is there any chance that we could conclude the testimony of this witness today?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Certainly. Then we'll have a break and resume at five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You knew, Mr. Rincic, Mr. Gotovina fairly well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: He was your -- your commander when you were in command of the logistics base?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you also have private trips to see him in 1995, around the time when you had private trips to see General Ademi, or maybe Colonel Ademi, at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: No. Because he wasn't there. At least he wasn't in Knin when I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did you ever --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the Defence of General Gotovina has an objection to my next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I do not know yet what your question. Neither do I know of the objection. So this is a very pleasant situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We -- I thank my colleague for bringing this up. I did question this line of inquiry. I don't know if it is appropriate. Maybe we can ask the witness if he speaks English, Judge, and I can possibly discuss this very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Rincic, do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do, though I can't be fully certain that I understand what is being said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe is always so clear in his language that, unfortunately, Mr. Rincic, I have to ask you to briefly leave the courtroom, because a matter will be discussed now which you're supposed not to be privy with. So if could you please follow the usher for a second, and then we hope that it will be as short as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, wouldn't it be best that we first hear what question Mr. Waespi had on his mind so that we can understand your objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The issue I wanted to raise with the witness was 65 ter 7423. That's a newspaper report about the fact that Mr. Rincic was considered a suspect in relation to the fugitive status of General Gotovina in 1994, and his house was raided, according to newspaper --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: -- 2004. Newspaper dates 27 September 2004. So according to the newspaper article, the house of the witness was raided and the investigation interrogation was ongoing and I want to ask the witness whether he was ever involved in helping General Gotovina to avoid justice and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If that's the question you'd like to put, we'd like to hear the objection. Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, the objection, Mr. President, is, with these documents, the good-faith basis when the Prosecution knows that the witness was brought in, questioned and released, and never charged. And what the Prosecution is attempting to do is somehow bring in some conspiratorial agreement between this witness and my client that goes into assisting General Gotovina during this time-frame. The fact of the matter is that the witness was questioned and released. So I don't quite understand, Mr. President, you know, this happens throughout the world people, where questioned and released, and does that the subject of inquiry in a criminal case? I suspect there is no court in the world that allows that, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I shouldn't say that, Mr. President. Maybe that is a little -- maybe that's a little over the top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- give us the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Certainly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- first the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Certainly there is no basis under these circumstances, Mr. President, to go into an issue where someone is brought into a station, questioned and released. It is an entirely different circumstance if the person is charged and there are criminal proceedings ongoing. That didn't happen here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Two points. First of all, my house has never been raided. I don't know about Mr. Kehoe's house --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yet. Yet. Your house hasn't been raided yet. That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Don't -- don't give up the hope, Mr. Waespi. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So, that is a pretty significant event, for which any police has to have whatever sense is probable cause. That's number one. Number two, it shows the -- indeed the connection between this witness and the accused, whom he volunteered to call "boys," and I think it is important to point that out to -- to the Trial Chamber. And he can explain what it was, for how long he has been interrogated, whether there was indeed probable cause, whether they found something or didn't find something, and I think it is only fair that I raise this issue with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me first briefly comment on the use of the term "boys." From the transcript, I think, and also from what I heard, there was a reference to "this boy." Apparently referring to Mr. Cermak. That's at least how I understood it. And I noted that when you later referred to that, you were talking in the plural. Whereas I understood it to be exclusively in relation to Mr. Cermak. Now, that, of course, may not be decisive, but at least, since Mr. -- since the issue apparently you're raising concerns not Mr. Cermak but only Mr. Gotovina that might -- the reference to "boy" might therefore not strictly apply.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: On this point, Mr. President, on line -- page 46, 24, the witness said: "... and not this boy over here." And I asked by saying "boy" you are referring to whom. And he answered, at least in the English interpretation: "I meant the Generals."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that's correct, then he moved to the plural which I then missed. Let me just ... Could you please repeat the page and --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Page 46.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 46, yes. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: [Indiscernible] the word "boy."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm there already in 46.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Page 47, line 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, one second. Yes, you're right. Again, there I understood -- it was my recollection that it was said "the General." But let's not -- it's not the core issue. Any further thing in response to what Mr. Kehoe said? Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to be of some assistance to the Chamber. As a native speaker, I heard the witness said "decki" which in the context of his speech should be translated as "guys," not "boys." So I think the proper translation of his word should be "guys," not "boys."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least atone other occasion his words were translated as "guys."

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps he used the same word there, but I noticed word "guys" was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Because it's a kind of, you know, slang speech, kind of colloquial speech. When someone is using the word "decki" in Croatian, literally the right translation is "boys" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, at least --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: -- but this is meant to be guys in that context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You propose that the translation in this context would be -- that's your proposition. I'm not commenting on you but you know that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the final authority for translations, and I never had any problem if someone would express views on sometimes improving or suggesting other translations, but what it is, is finally in the hands -- but we have carefully listened to your observations, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It's kind of fine-tuning translation, Your Honour, if I may say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but that doesn't change the matter, that even for fine-tuned translation, that the Chamber finally relies on the CLSS --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and interpreters who are doing such a great job here. But I do understand that you, as a native-speaking person, have raised some issues in relation to the use of the word "boys" in translation of the word you just mentioned. That's on the record. That's clear. Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just one last comment with regard to this line of inquiry. This is a witness for the Cermak Defence, and given this is the Cermak Defence, what's the relevance with regard to General Gotovina? And clearly this is being brought to bear during the Gotovina case if -- or against General Gotovina. And consequently given the state of the proceedings it is simply not relevant given the fact that this was a witness put up by General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although the evidence this witness gives is not excluded from being evaluated in the case against Mr. Gotovina, or is it your view that it is?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No. My view is that I think that if the Prosecution wanted to go into something along this line on their case somehow going into, you know, some type of conspiratorial agreement to -- while General Gotovina was a fugitive, then that is something they have put on in their case. I'm not saying that the Court or the Chamber should dice and splice each individual item concerning what is put forth by the respective Defences, but this is clearly, clearly being pointed at my client.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's clear. Mr. Kay, it is your witness who is cross-examined by Mr. Waespi --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and is there anything you would like to add because I first wanted to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour, having now been enlightened on the issue which I did not know was going to be raised. This is called a so-called credibility issue and the fact is that the Prosecution are relying on a newspaper report rather than source material that defines the so-called credibility issue, which is the fact that there was some sort of police inquiry out of which no charges arose. In my submission, that puts to rest the credibility issue, as far as this matter goes. I must say, in my code of conduct where I come from, you're not allowed to do this kind of thing. If you have such information, it in fact does not go to a witness's credibility and it offends against the bar council's codes of conduct. We had an example of that yesterday with the particular witness where some information was found from somewhere or other, I'm not actually sure where even now, and we had a big inquiry and now the witness came out and said, Well, actually I won this case and there was no finding against me. What is happening here is people's characters are being blackened before this Court than is actually in opposition to people giving evidence. I can tell the Court that, that people are concerned about what goes on in such a way, and it's a deterrent for the truth to come out in this Court. In my submission, the Court has duty to consider the interests of witnesses. This is just one such a situation, where the so-called credibility issue amounted to nothing. It is not a credibility issue because the authorities in the police did not charge this man with anything. The fact that you may be arrested, questioned or your house searched is a matter of criminal procedure. That does not mean that are you a man of bad character or that you are a man who has committed any sort of offence. Quite the opposite, in fact, because nothing further came from it, and the Prosecution know that as a fact. But in trying to use other materials, what is happening here, in my submission, is not good for justice and not right for witnesses, and does not assist these proceedings or show them in a good light.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, could I ask you how familiar you are with the follow-up of the raid and the questioning of Mr. Rincic? Have you inquired into whether there was ever a prosecution? If not, do you know the reasons why he was not prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We made a Google search, and found another article in Slobodna Dalmacija, the next day, where Mr. Rincic kind of admits to what happened, and he said that he was later released, he said in a phone interview to this newspaper, and accepted that he was -- that police interview with him lasted all night, and that -- and I just quote from this article: "They explored the possible connection to my people who helped hide Ante Gotovina," and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's not an answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But that's as far as I could -- I did my inquiries, no more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and you didn't ask for, I hardly dare to say, for the Official Note which may have been taken at that moment in order to give further information about what he may have told and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That could be -- sometimes after witnesses leave we make follow-up RFAs and this could be, depending on whether you allow me to question the witness on what his answers are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, with all due respect to counsel on this, and I don't want to speak for Mr. Kay, but I do believe this witness's name has been disclosed to the Prosecution for some time. I will turn to my learned friend. I don't know exactly what the date was but I do recall it being sometime in the late spring, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When we filed our Rule 65 ter list of witnesses, which was in March -- May. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber will not allow you to put this question to the witness, Mr. Waespi. However, there's another thing that came to our mind, which is the following. Yesterday -- or, yes, I think it was yesterday, where the witness was able to explain that -- how this whole matter ended up in court, an option would be, the Chamber is not insisting on it, but I could ask the witness that, During the break it was brought to our attention that once your house was raided and you were questioned, is there anything you'd like to bring to our attention, in relation to that? And if he then starts explaining why he was not prosecuted, then I would think it would even be good to know that. I would not immediately expect him to say, I was questioned and, of course, what I did was to assist Mr. Gotovina. That's not the question I consider most -- the answer mostly likely to be expected. That came to my mind. I'm, at the same time, hesitant to do such a thing, but I'm seeking here the input of the parties and the ruling is clear, we will not allow Mr. Waespi to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I understand that Your Honour -- Your Honours' questions in this regard, but this issue is directed towards my client and it has real -- at this point, absolutely no relevance to these proceedings so -- and given the fact that nothing happened and we don't have anything else, we would object and ask the Chamber just to preclude the Prosecution from asking the question and move on to another subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Can I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Other parties. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Again, I think it's a relevance issue. Once we look at this for what it's worth, Your Honour, and in my submission, the Court really should be focussed on his evidence rather this kind of side issue in relation to character --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, anything you would like to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The relevance issue is, as pointed out by Mr. Kay, the character and the credibility of the witness, and that is not a side issue. That is as important the truthfulness, the transparency of where these witnesses are coming from, the allegiance to the accused, to anybody, is very important for Your Honours. And I understand I'm not allowed to go into that, but the relevance issue is certainly not the crucial point, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Having consulted my colleagues, the Chamber cannot conclude that there's no relevance at all in such a question. At the same time, irrelevant -- irrelevance is not such that I would proceed along the lines that came to my mind for five seconds and which I shared with you, so, therefore, we'll invite the witness to come back and you may move on, Mr. Waespi, with your next topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, the witness will come back into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Rincic, sometimes lawyers --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- need close to ten minutes to find out that they have no further questions for you, and you had to wait all this time. Mr. Waespi has concluded his cross-examination. I'll now address the other parties whether there is any need to re-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Rincic. I just would like to ask you about some of the questions that you were -- specifically questions that you were asked by Mr. Waespi concerning assistance to railway workers and matters of that nature. I would like to show you 65 ter 4451.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, just for the record, this is -- this has -- parts of this have been put in evidence already. It is a -- the log-book of the 72nd Military Police Battalion. All of it has not been translated, I have to guide the Court in that regard. But I would like the -- excuse me, yes. It's the Knin Company. I have just been advised that the 72nd Military Police Battalion -- and if we could as part of this, if we could put page 5 of the B/C/S and page 1 of the third translation on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you three entries here, Mr. Rincic, and then just ask you a question. You can see the entry for the 72nd Military Police Battalion, the Knin company, on 12th/13th of August, 1995, at the top, entry 1. Request by the Knin garrison to escort railway employees to Zitnice. If we can turn our attention to page 8 in the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just try to understand what you're putting. We're talking about 12th/13th of August, yes. I would just like to read what you put to the witness so that I --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is entry number 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would let me read.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could turn to page 8 in the B/C/S and page 4 in this third translation. And at the bottom block for August the 16th, get the English. We have the bottom block, yes, towards the bottom is the 16th, and I believe that is a request from Mr. Rincic for military police to provide security for the Croatian post and telecommunications employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I believe you referred to that previously, Mr. Rincic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And we have -- if can turn to page 10 in the B/C/S and page 6 in this third translation. And if we look at the bottom of that page -- the first -- yes, that's it, good. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And if we look at the entry number 2 there for the 18th of August, we have you, Mr. Rincic, requesting five or six policemen to be sent to secure the HZ, being the Croatian railway employees. Now, Mr. Rincic, when you were talking about those types of requests for the military police, are these the types of matters that you were referring to as we see in this log?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, we will to offer 65 ter 4451, this third translation, which, again, is a -- in the 12 pages in this there are translations so the Court can see the context of these entries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you already assign a number for this document to be MFI'd. The reason for that, Mr. Kehoe, being that we have carefully finds what exactly is selected, what is evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is no issue about admission as such but that's rather to clearly define what we have in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1684, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. One additional question in relation to this, Mr. Rincic, we see in this entry it says: "Rincic ZM." Have idea what that stands for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, probably the individual who wrote this assumed that I was a soldier. Perhaps that was his understanding of who I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not everyone was aware of the fact that I was in charge of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Rincic, I didn't ask you about any thoughts behind the person who may have written this but what the letters ZM could stand for.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To me, it seems -- Zdenko is my first name, so there you have a Z there, but I wouldn't be able to tell you what exactly this means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is no M in your first name, is there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you imagine any other meaning of ZM? Was that a usual abbreviation for something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, normally that's how I sign my name, Rincic Zdenko. Perhaps he mistook my name for something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, did it come to your mind in the last minute or last minute and a half that it could also be Zborno Mjesto?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. Perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked you whether it came to your mind. I think you can answer that question if ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It did, but it doesn't make sense that this is what it should state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer. Any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Nothing further, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Kinis has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Mr. Rincic, in your statement in paragraph 28 and paragraph 30, you mentioned how many tasks you were carried out under leadership of General Cermak. My question is -- maybe it will consist by two parts. The first is: I would like to know who participate in this activities? Was there some labour force or was there -- was there soldiers who participate in these activities just cleaning up and transport and feeding and so on and so forth. And the second question is: Who finances this operations, really? Do you have some budget for -- for this garrison command, or how it was organised at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Let me be specific. I recollect that when it came to the clearing up of the streets in Knin that were overflowing with rubble and for the cleaning up of apartment blocks and flats, with coordination from Mr. Cermak, volunteers of the Red Cross were engaged, as well as various associations from Zagreb. These were mostly women who were engaged in cleaning. The support was provided by the civilian police, in terms of lorries. Others, who were able to, also provided support. Assistance was sought from units, and even from UNPROFOR itself. They provided some support too. UNPROFOR was stationed in the vicinity of Knin, in barracks. As for financial support, when needed, we sought assistance from public utility companies from the town of Sibenik to step in, the town of Sibenik being the closest, as well as from the towns of Zadar and Split. In other words, public utility companies of the surrounding towns, of the towns nearby, were the ones that were most involved in the cleaning exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KINIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Rincic, I have a few questions for you about the railways. You were asked whether it was the Knin-Gracac railway. And you said: "Also" -- that's at least what was -- what I remember. And I'm just checking that. The problem is that the word "also" does not appear in the WordWheel. Are you aware of any other railway repair jobs that were done under security provided by the military police?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: The entire railway line from Slunj to Knin, which had previously been occupied, was in a bad state of repair in many places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: And the task was given for the whole line to be repaired, not just for the Gracac-Knin section to be repaired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I was specifically asking about security provided not only for that portion but for other railway works, or repairs as well.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Really, I can't remember at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how do I have to understand the security? Because I take it, were they working 24 hours a day, or was this a day shift? And how was this security then organised, in relation to these repair jobs?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: It was mostly day shifts. They did not work during the night, so they did not have to be secured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And would, then, the security report in the morning in Knin, or at the relevant portion of the railway line, or ...

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Well, it depended on where they came from, where the repair workers came from. If they came from Split, as they were entering Knin, they would meet up with them and then they headed together towards the point that was being repaired. If they came from the northern part, then they would meet perhaps -- if they, for example, came from Karlovac, from the Croatian railway branch in Karlovac, then they would meet up somewhere in the north, near Udbina, which is north of Knin, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now would -- providing such security, was that more or less a routine or was it exceptional?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: It was exceptional; it was not a matter of routine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And in total, how many -- how many days -- I don't know perhaps the right English expression, but how many man days, that is, how many -- if we're talking about three days, five men, that makes 15 man days. How much was, in total, involved in the security on these railway lines? Could you give an estimate, if you know.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: During the period covering 15/16 and 17 days, the security was needed for seven to eight days, even more than that. Even longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you said three to four people.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I was not the only person in charge of the repair of the railway line. The area was simply too large, and it covered over 100 kilometres. There were several individuals involved in the task. Mr. Cermak also looked after the railway line, and it was not that I knew everything, every detail of the exercise. The managing director of the Croatian railways and the executive directors of the Croatian railway branches in the neighbouring towns, we were all involved in that huge task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was a request for security for this type of work ever denied by the military police? I mean not postponed but denied.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, it didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move to another subject. You talked about that meeting, where, apparently, the letter sent by General Forand was discussed and where you said that Mr. Cermak expressed that this should stop or requested that it should stop, and when asked, What should stop, you included killing. And then you gave one answer, which I would like to briefly further explore with you. You said, when asked who "they" were, they who had to stop. You said: "Certain civilians, they believed that" -- no. You were talking about certain civilians being killed and then you said: "They believed that they were soldiers," and you were referring to the perpetrators of the killing. You said: "They believed." Then you were asked by Mr. Waespi who "they "were. And then you said: "If I would know, I would have told those who ought to know." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, if you do not know who the perpetrators are, how could you know that they thought that the civilians that were killed, that they believed that they were soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Maybe you didn't understand me properly. That's what I believed at the moment when I heard the information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But my question is: You express your views on what those who apparently committed killings, what they believed; whereas, you don't know who they are.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I said that when I heard the information, I believed that those persons, those individuals, had believed that they were killing soldiers. It would not have made any sense for them to be killing civilians. Having put all in that way, I suppose that what I believed at the time was wrong, within that context, because it turned out later that things were actually different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you explain that last -- what was different?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Later on, I learned, or I understood, that people who were killed were not soldiers but some other individuals. And that's why I said that if I knew who had killed them, I would have turned them in immediately. If I had known who they were, I would have turned them in immediately, at the moment when I learned what they had done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Rincic, your initial answer was, about the killings to be stopped, that these were civilians killed by persons who believed they were soldiers. Your last answer, in which you say it turned out to be different, you said they turned out to be civilians. That's not in way different from what you earlier said, and I'm exploring what is at the basis of your testimony where you say that persons unknown killed civilians but, as you said, they believed them to be soldiers. How could you know, or how could we know, if you don't know who they are, whether they initially killed civilians, or whether they killed civilians, believing that they were soldiers? How can we know; how can you know?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: I was convinced that there were no civilians around Knin, that the only people who might have been there were some soldiers who had stayed behind. During those two or three initial days, I could not even believe that there were any civilians there. I believed that all civilians had already left. At least that's what could be heard on the grape-vine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. A final brief subject. Did you move around in town the first day when you were in Knin?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever see household appliances not in apartment buildings but outside apartment buildings? And I'm not talking refrigerators but, for example, television sets, perhaps washing machines, furniture? Did you ever see that on the -- on the streets?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What did you think about that? What came to your mind when you saw that?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Just like we said before, that people were leaving Knin, people who had resided there, and that whatever they could not carry, they threw out of their apartments in order to destroy those things. They didn't simply want anybody who was going to move into their apartments to make use of those things. That's what occurred to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do I have to understand that if, for example, we're talking about television sets, they were all destroyed? They are not perhaps still functioning?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: The fact is that you could not even spend a night in Knin, because in those abandoned flats, you could not see any furniture. There were no appliances. Everything had either been taken away or thrown out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me then -- do we agree that you can see the difference if a television set is a thrown out of the window or when it's put on the pavement. Would you agree that that can be seen, the difference between?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Because if you throw out something, if you throw it out of the window, then you break it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I then take it that, in view of your explanation, that television sets you may have seen on the pavement were all destroyed, were not, from the outside, looking as if they were still in a condition that they possibly could be used?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: They were broken. They could not be used. At least that's what I could see. That's my assessment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. One very last item. You told us about the Tvik factory where, as I understood you well, half products, casings were found. Did you find any ammunition which was already ready to be sold, so fully produced, not a half product but in its end stage? Did you find any of those?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't find any such products.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because if you see a half products in a situation as you described, then Mr. Waespi asked you, but it looked rather obvious to me that if in such a factory you find these half products and that is apparently where they are produced or will be further produced. Now, talking about production, I wondered, but please give your comment, that, with a -- perhaps not fully unexpected but at least with a military operation which came to some extent as a surprise, the time not being known, it would surprise me if all of the fully produced ammunition could have been taken out in time under those circumstances. Do you have any explanation as to why you found only half products and where nothing fully produced was found?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: They needed any finished products, to use them against us as we were advancing towards Knin. They had ample time to take everything. We didn't find a single pistol, a single gun. We didn't find any weapons. They had taken everything away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Were weapons produced as well in the Tvik factory, according to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: No. There was no technology in place to produce weapons. Only ammunition could be made there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm trying to understand your answer where you said well, they had all time because we didn't find any weapons; whereas, you say weapons were not produced there.

utterances.speaker: ZDENKO RINCIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, I have a lot of experience, and I saw a lot of things, not only in Knin but among people who worked even civilians were armed. I believe that even those civilian workers in the factory had been armed and that's why I said what I did. I suppose that in the area both troops and civilians carried weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Have the questions by the Bench triggered any need for further questions. Then, Mr. Rincic, this concludes your evidence in this court. I would like to thank you very much for coming a rather long way to The Hague and for having answered the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there are no other procedural issues to be raised, then we'll adjourn, and we will resume tomorrow, Thursday, the 1st of October, at quarter past 2.00, in Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 1st of October, 2009, at 2.15 p.m. 21 22 23 24 25
